clue.text: Sounds like a Steinbeckian take on Portnoy's Complaint

indicators.note: the clue asks for something said aloud that resembles a Steinbeck title, so pronunciation is the signal

parts.note: a Steinbeckian title here is his Dust Bowl novel about the Joad family's grapes and wrath

explanation.surface: A literary jest: how John Steinbeck might have retitled a famous comic novel of sexual guilt.
explanation.walkthrough: Portnoy's Complaint is by Philip Roth; his 'gripes' are the complaint, and the phrase is a near-rhyme on Steinbeck's 1939 novel title.
explanation.definitionFit: Portnoy's Complaint is Philip Roth's novel, so a punning version of it is a set of grumbles belonging to its author.

clue.text: The morning after the first of the Georges left his house

indicators.note: left in the sense of departed: the letter named goes out of the word before it

parts.note: the morning after a night's drinking is a hangover

indicators.note: the first of the Georges points to the opening letter of that word only

explanation.surface: King George I wakes up hungover and walks out of his family home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like a past tense of leave describing George's exit, but it removes G (the first letter of Georges) from HANGOVER.
explanation.definitionFit: George I of Great Britain belonged to the German royal dynasty of that electorate, which became the reigning house.

clue.text: Most of energy, manic energy, dissipated in Equus, for example

indicators.note: dissipated means scattered, so the gathered letters are spread and reformed
most of the word means all but its final letter

parts.note: taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A frenzied burst of vigour spent in a performance of Peter Shaffer's horse-blinding play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' drops Y from ENERGY to leave ENERG; with MANIC and E, 'dissipated' rearranges the letters. Equus is also a play title, which the surface exploits.
explanation.definitionFit: In biological classification Equus is the genus label of horses, the first word of a scientific binomial.

clue.text: Linguistic peculiarity policeman picked up on island

indicators.note: in a down entry, picked up means lifted so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: DI is a Detective Inspector, a police rank
IOM abbreviates the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: An odd turn of phrase heard by a constable while stationed on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' places the reversed policeman above the island in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An expression peculiar to a language, whose meaning cannot be worked out from its words, is a classic example of a linguistic quirk.

clue.text: Character to ward off current Turkish mister

parts.note: EF is the spelt-out name of the letter F, a written character
to fend off is to ward off
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: Someone tries to repel an electrical current with a protective letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' means a letter of the alphabet here, given as its spoken name.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is a Turkish courtesy form of address for a man of standing, like sir or mister.

clue.text: Painter's excessive old representation of angel

parts.note: OTT is short for over the top, meaning excessive

indicators.note: a representation of the word rearranges its letters into a new form

explanation.surface: A critic calls an artist's ornate old picture of an angel overdone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Painter's' is read as 'Painter is'; OTT and O are followed by NAGEL, the letters of ANGEL rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a twentieth-century German artist from Berlin known for scenes of working-class life.

clue.text: Scandi rug described by Margery Allingham

indicators.note: the name described by these words contains the needed letters within its spelling

explanation.surface: A Scandinavian carpet appears in a description by the detective novelist Margery Allingham.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across the join of margeRY Allingham; Allingham was an English writer of Golden Age detective fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a knotted, thick-piled Scandinavian floor covering, originally from Sweden.

clue.text: What three little girls found when they got well

definitions.text: What three little girls found when they got well

parts.words: What three little girls found when they got well
parts.note: in Alice in Wonderland the Dormouse tells of three sisters who lived at the bottom of a well filled with a sticky syrup, so 'got well' means went to that well, not recovered

explanation.surface: Three small girls recover from an illness and discover something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got well' suggests recovering from illness; the Dormouse's tale at the Mad Hatter's tea party is the key.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dormouse's sisters drew a dark syrup, golden or black, from their well, which is what they found there.

clue.text: Apparently prolific writer, one that's French, no?

parts.note: A is the indefinite article, meaning one
non is the French word for no

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a famously productive author is a Frenchman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's' is a link. The definition is a joke: unsigned works are attributed to this abbreviation, so it seems to have written a vast amount.
explanation.definitionFit: Countless works of unknown authorship are credited to anonymous, so that label appears to be the most productive author of all.

clue.text: "- stones. / Hills seeming to strain / And cry out / In labour." (Ted Hughes)

definitions.text: "- stones. / Hills seeming to strain / And cry out / In labour." (Ted Hughes)

parts.words: - stones. / Hills seeming to strain / And cry out / In labour.
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing adjective before stones comes from a Ted Hughes poem in which hills are pictured as passionate and straining

explanation.surface: A fragment of Ted Hughes's verse with its opening word blanked out for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: Pure literary knowledge: the word completing the line is the one Hughes uses for stones besotted with love.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word describes stones overcome with passion, the sense of being madly in love or besotted.

clue.text: Novel or morality play

definitions.meaning: a 2006 Philip Roth novel about an ordinary man facing death
the fifteenth-century English allegorical drama of a common man summoned by Death

explanation.definitionFit: The title names both the medieval allegory of the ordinary person and Roth's novel borrowing that title.

clue.text: Subtlety that's absent in Faulkner's Nancy going to church

indicators.note: in means the letter for absent is placed inside the word for Faulkner's Nancy

parts.note: Nancy Mannigoe is the nun of Faulkner's Requiem for a Nun
A is a standard abbreviation for absent, as on a register
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A fine point missing from a Faulkner character's trip to church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's' and 'going to' are links; Faulkner's Requiem for a Nun names Nancy as its nun, a fact the solver needs.
explanation.definitionFit: A shade of difference or delicate distinction in meaning is a subtlety.

clue.text: Ovid's poem broadcast at Maria and Rosa?

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so these letters are spread and reformed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ovid's love poetry is read out on air to two women named Maria and Rosa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' joins the fodder and gives no letters; AT MARIA plus ROSA rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Latin title of the Roman poet's didactic work on the art of love.

clue.text: Jiminy! One's no good at sport

parts.note: Jiminy Cricket is the conscience in Disney's Pinocchio
I is the Roman numeral one, with 's as is

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at someone's sporting incompetence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jiminy!' looks like a mild oath but names the Disney insect; cricket is the bat-and-ball game popular in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes taking part in the bat-and-ball game, so it means engaged in a particular sport.

clue.text: Novel Shakespearian stage direction?

definitions.meaning: Philip Roth's 2007 novel, the last to feature Nathan Zuckerman
Hamlet's dead father leaves the stage, so a script would instruct the spirit to depart

explanation.definitionFit: Roth took the title from the printed instruction in Hamlet telling the phantom king to leave the stage.

clue.text: Beatles' Let It Be finally remastered — Let It Be

indicators.note: remastered means remade, so the collected letters are put into a new order
finally takes the last letter of each word of the band and album title

explanation.surface: A new remaster of the Beatles' last album is released.
explanation.walkthrough: The final letters S, T, T, E are rearranged; the definition is the proofreader's instruction to leave text as it was.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin proofreading mark means let it stand, instructing that a deleted word be kept.

clue.text: Bryant's pupil, according to Russell

parts.note: in Willy Russell's play Educating ..., the tutor Frank Bryant teaches a working-class hairdresser

explanation.surface: A teacher named Bryant has a student, as told by someone called Russell.
explanation.walkthrough: Willy Russell is the playwright; Frank Bryant is his Open University tutor.
explanation.definitionFit: Russell's hairdresser who studies literature under Frank goes by this chosen first name.

clue.text: Jones, popular with a girl

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
Diana is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Someone surnamed Jones is a hit with a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins the pieces. 'Jones' is the definition: the archaeologist hero of the film series.
explanation.definitionFit: Harrison Ford's whip-wielding archaeologist in the film series has this as his first name.

clue.text: One meeting a new Belgian writer

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a Fleming is a Flemish-speaking Belgian

explanation.surface: Someone is introduced to a recently arrived author from Belgium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meeting' joins the pieces. 'Belgian' looks like an adjective for the writer, but it gives a noun for a native of Flanders.
explanation.definitionFit: He was the British author who created James Bond.

clue.text: Novel's fate

definitions.meaning: Philip Roth's 2010 novel set during a polio epidemic
an inescapable agent of downfall or retribution

explanation.definitionFit: Roth's final novel takes as its title the Greek goddess of retribution, the inescapable downfall.

clue.text: Managed to return with speed to tell the tale

indicators.note: to return means to go back, so the word for managed reads backwards

parts.note: ran means managed, as in ran a business
rate is a speed

explanation.surface: Someone gets back quickly enough to recount what happened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins the pieces: NAR (RAN reversed) followed by RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To recount a story or give an account of events is to tell it.

clue.text: Amount of work needed to gain an honour from this famous Swede

indicators.note: to gain means to take in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: an erg is a unit of work in physics
DBE is Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire, an honour

explanation.surface: A famous Swede must put in effort before earning a decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needed' is a link; 'to gain' signals the container. The honour is a British damehood, and 'Amount of work' is the physics unit, not a workload.
explanation.definitionFit: Stefan, the Swedish tennis player, won six Grand Slam singles titles including Wimbledon twice.

clue.text: Threatening Dracula's mistress, right?

parts.note: Mina Harker is the woman the Count pursues in Bram Stoker's novel
a Tory belongs to the political right in Britain

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether Count Dracula's lover is menacing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right' looks like a tag question but means politically right-wing; Tory is the nickname for a British Conservative.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a formal synonym for menacing, describing words or looks that carry a threat.

clue.text: Beautiful maid, friend of Falstaff and perhaps Hal at first

parts.note: Nym is one of Falstaff's cronies in Shakespeare

indicators.note: at first takes the opening letter of each of the two words before it

explanation.surface: A lovely girl is a companion of Falstaff and maybe Prince Hal too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hal' looks like another Shakespeare character in the scene, but only its first letter is used, with that of 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: In mythology these are lovely young female spirits of nature, so the word means a beautiful young woman.

clue.text: Perhaps flower that Browning longed to see on his pear-tree

definitions.text: Perhaps flower that Browning longed to see on his pear-tree

parts.words: Perhaps flower that Browning longed to see on his pear-tree
parts.note: Robert Browning's Home-Thoughts, from Abroad longs for England in spring, after April when the next month follows, with his blossomed pear-tree in the hedge

explanation.surface: A homesick poet yearns for flowers on his own fruit tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' flags that the bloom is an example; hawthorn flowers carry this name in England.
explanation.definitionFit: Browning pictures the spring month after April, and hawthorn bloom of that month is the English example.

clue.text: What Scrooge offered for a turkey for his employee

definitions.text: What Scrooge offered for a turkey
definitions.meaning: a shilling in old British slang; Scrooge promises a boy a shilling to fetch the poulterer
Scrooge's clerk in A Christmas Carol is Cratchit, known by this first name

explanation.definitionFit: Old British slang for a shilling coincides with the first name of Scrooge's clerk Cratchit.

clue.text: Novel performance of Sunday In the Park With George?

definitions.meaning: Philip Roth's 1995 novel about the puppeteer Mickey Sabbath

definitions.text: performance of Sunday In the Park With George?
definitions.meaning: a staging of a musical with Sunday in its title is jokingly a show of the day of rest
